key: G major, ending in E major
question: How does a symphony end in a key it never began in?
intro: A soprano sings a child’s vision of heaven — a feast of saints, lambs, bread and music — in a song Mahler wrote in 1892 and made the goal of the whole symphony. Listen for the sleigh bells from the first movement and for the key it ends in, which is not G.

sections.label: Verse 1 · Wir genießen die himmlischen Freuden
Verse 3 · Gut’ Kräuter, Rehbock, Fische
sections.mNote: first melody returns, with faster hunting-and-fishing episodes

sections.label: Verse 4 · Kein’ Musik ist ja nicht auf Erden

cues.title: Clarinet, horn and harp
cues.text: Marked “Sehr behaglich” — very comfortable — the finale opens with a clarinet, a horn and the harp over muted violas and cellos. The violins and basses wait. The tune is made of fragments from the first movement.
cues.evidence: Full score (IMSLP70999), PDF p. 102 (printed p. 328): the first bars are scored for clarinet, horn, harp and muted viola and cello. Basinger says the woodwinds trade fragments that recall first-movement themes: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: the file opens at −27.8 dB and attack density is 0.0–0.4 per second to 0:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A warning to the conductor
cues.text: Mahler heads the movement with a note to the conductor: “It is of the greatest importance that the singer be extremely discreetly accompanied.” The orchestra must serve the child’s voice, not cover it.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 102 (printed p. 328): “Anmerkung für den Dirigenten: Es ist von höchster Wichtigkeit, dass die Sängerin äusserst discret begleitet wird” with the English translation printed beneath.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Oboes, cor anglais and bassoons join
cues.text: Oboes, cor anglais, bass clarinet and bassoons enter in short, soft phrases, the basses pluck, and a flurry of flutes and clarinets rises with a slight slowing before the voice begins.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 102–103: oboe, cor anglais, bass clarinet and bassoon staves enter in the first page; “Poco rit.” and a flute and clarinet flurry on the second. Report: boundary at 0:14 (novelty 0.57) and relative level −11 dB at 0:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The child sings
cues.text: The soprano enters at rehearsal 1, “a tempo”: “Wir genießen die himmlischen Freuden” — we enjoy heavenly pleasures. Mahler’s direction in the score is to sing with childlike, serene expression, absolutely without parody.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 104 (printed p. 330): rehearsal 1 “a tempo”, the vocal line and the note “Singstimme mit kindlich heiterem Ausdruck; durchaus ohne Parodie!”. Report: relative level falls from −11 dB at 0:25 to −20.7 dB at 0:30 as the voice enters over a thinner texture.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A violin-filled sky
cues.text: The poem comes from Des Knaben Wunderhorn. Mahler’s title, “Das himmlische Leben”, is his own: the anthology calls it “Der Himmel hängt voll Geigen”, the sky hangs full of violins, an idiom akin to “there’s not a cloud in the sky”.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s introduction explains the title and the idiom: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Angelic life, dancing words
cues.text: At rehearsal 2, “Fliessend” — flowing — the music quickens for “Wir führen ein englisches Leben” and on to “Wir tanzen und springen, wir hüpfen und singen”: we dance and leap, we hop and sing. Attacks jump to nearly three a second.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 106–107 (printed pp. 332–333): rehearsal 2 “Fliessend” at “Wir führen ein englisches Leben”, then the dancing lines and “Nicht schleppen”. Basinger describes the increase in rhythmic activity at this text: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: attack density is 2.8 per second at 1:10 and brightness is about 2090 Hz.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A hymn for Saint Peter
cues.text: Mahler sets the verse’s last line, “Sanct Peter im Himmel sieht zu” — Saint Peter watches from heaven — as a solemn, chorale-like phrase. Strings are muted and horns soft, and the level sinks to about −28 dB.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 108 (printed p. 334): “Sanct Peter im Himmel sieht zu!”, “Plötzlich zurückhaltend”, muted strings and horns. Basinger describes the final line as a solemn chorale: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: relative level is −28.1 dB at 1:45 with E minor estimates at 1:40–1:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sleigh bells in the minor
cues.text: Suddenly brisk — “Plötzlich frisch bewegt” — the first movement’s sleigh-bell figure returns in the minor, now with real sleigh bells. A footnote insists that this tempo be faster than the matching passages in the first movement.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 108–109 (printed pp. 334–335): “Plötzlich frisch bewegt” with the footnote that the tempo must be faster than at the corresponding passages in the first movement; sleigh-bell, triangle and cymbal staves. Basinger describes the transformed bells in the minor: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: boundary at 1:50 (novelty 0.71), brightness 2891 Hz, level rising from −28.1 to −10.8 dB.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The butcher Herod waits
cues.text: In the second verse John lets go of his little lamb, Herod the butcher waits, and Saint Luke slaughters the oxen. Mahler’s child sings of this with the same serenity; the feast, the Mahler Foundation notes, comes at the animals’ expense.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page notes that the heavenly feast takes place at the expense of animals, including a sacrificed lamb: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-4-das-himmlische-leben-sehr-behaglich/ . The poem text is quoted in the Mahler Foundation page and the Utah guide.
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Bleating and bellowing
cues.text: Over the second verse’s new melody, Basinger hears the oboe imitating a bleating sheep and the bass clarinet a bellowing ox, as the text turns to the slaughter of lamb and ox. The bells have stopped.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the oboe and bass clarinet figures and the new soprano melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: attack density is about 2.0–2.2 per second at 2:25–2:35. The player assignments are the guide’s, not verified against this recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The angels bake the bread
cues.text: The verse ends with “Die Englein, die backen das Brot” — the angels bake the bread — and the Saint Peter chorale returns like a refrain. Listen for the same hushed, hymn-like phrase as at the end of the first verse.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the second verse ending with angels baking bread and the chorale returning as a refrain: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: relative level is −10.5 dB at 2:55 and falls to −17.5 dB at 3:00; E minor estimates read r 0.82 at 2:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A bell interlude
cues.text: A short instrumental interlude brings back the distorted sleigh bells. The level dips at 3:05 and the brightness spikes again at 3:10 before the soprano resumes.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the distorted sleigh bells returning in a short instrumental interlude before the third verse: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: relative level is −27.1 dB at 3:05 and −10.7 dB at 3:10, with brightness 2763 Hz at 3:10.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: The first melody returns
cues.text: The third verse, “Gut’ Kräuter von allerhand Arten”, takes up the movement’s first melody again for the herbs, asparagus and beans of the heavenly garden. Verses one and three share this tune; verse two had its own.
cues.evidence: Basinger says the movement’s initial melody recurs in the third verse: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: key estimates read G major at 3:20 (r 0.82) and 3:30 (r 0.87), with D major (r 0.77) between at 3:25; attack density 0.2–0.6 per second.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Deer, hare and darting fish
cues.text: As roebuck and hare run down the open street, the tempo quickens and the sleigh bells ring briefly. Rapid swirling figures then suggest the fish that Saint Peter chases, with attacks reaching nearly four a second near 4:00.
cues.evidence: Basinger describes the acceleration, the brief sleigh bells and the swirling figuration for the fish: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: attack density is 1.4 at 3:40, 2.8 at 3:45 and 3.8 at 4:00; brightness 2203–2394 Hz at 3:55–4:05.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Saint Martha is the cook
cues.text: “Sanct Martha die Köchin muß sein” — Saint Martha must be the cook — and the refrain swells into an extended restatement. The key estimates lean to the minor, then the sound ebbs away.
cues.evidence: Basinger says the image of Saint Martha cooking prompts an extended restatement of the refrain: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: relative level is −13.6 dB at 4:15 and −13.2 dB at 4:25, then −21.6 dB at 4:30; estimates read G minor at 4:15 (r 0.77) and 4:25–4:35 (r 0.76–0.85), with D minor (r 0.69) at 4:20.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: A song becomes a symphony
cues.text: Mahler set this poem for voice and piano on 10 February 1892 and orchestrated it that March. He nearly made it the finale of the Third Symphony, as “Was mir das Kind erzählt”, then built a whole symphony towards it.
cues.evidence: Basinger gives the dates of the voice-and-piano version and the symphonic transcription: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation describes the planned Third Symphony title and the decision to make the song the Fourth’s goal: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: The bells ring again
cues.text: Another sleigh-bell episode begins the last section, fortissimo and brilliant, then fades to pp. At its end the key signature changes to four sharps: the music is about to leave G for good.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 122 (printed p. 348): “Schellen” and triangle, ff fading to pp, and a new signature of four sharps at the system’s end. Basinger describes another sleigh-bell episode initiating the final section: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: a strong boundary at 4:54 (novelty 0.86), brightness 2993 Hz at 4:55.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll
cues.text: At rehearsal 12 the marking is “Tempo I. Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss” — very tender and mysterious to the end. Muted strings and harp triplets sustain it, and the key is E major.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 123 (printed p. 349): rehearsal 12, “Tempo I. Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss”, “mit Dämpfer”, harp triplets, four-sharp signature. Report: boundary at 5:08 (novelty 0.56), relative level −29.4 dB at 5:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra alone
cues.text: For nearly a minute the orchestra plays the new melody without the singer: flute and cor anglais over harp and muted strings. Listen to how sparse it is; attacks almost vanish.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 123–124: no vocal line until rehearsal 13; flute and cor anglais carry the melody over harp triplets. Report: attack density is 0.0 per second across 5:10–6:00 and key estimates read E minor (r 0.57–0.86) throughout 5:10–6:00. Those are estimates and do not confirm the written E major, which comes from the four-sharp signature in the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Music unlike any on earth
cues.text: At rehearsal 13 the soprano takes up the new tune: “Kein’ Musik ist ja nicht auf Erden” — there is no music on earth to compare with ours. The strings stay muted, “immer Dämpfer”, down at ppp.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 124 (printed p. 350): rehearsal 13, the vocal line “Kein Mu-sik ist ja nicht auf Erden, die uns’rer vergli-chen kann wer-den”, “immer Dämpfer”, ppp. Report: boundary at 6:00 (novelty 0.63), relative level −23.0 to −25.0 dB through 6:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Eleven thousand virgins dare to dance
cues.text: Around 6:28, the finale’s strongest boundary, the harmony shifts: the key estimates pass through B major and F♯ major and minor. At this point in the score the soprano sings of the eleven thousand virgins who dare to dance.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 125 (printed p. 351): vocal line “Elf-tau-send Jungfrau-en zu tan-zen sich trau-en!”. Report: strongest boundary at 6:28 (novelty 1.00), key estimates read B major (r 0.51) at 6:25, F♯ major (r 0.62) at 6:30 and F♯ minor (r 0.73) at 6:35. The match between this boundary and the sung line is by page proportion only.
cues.how: Located by measuring this recording.

cues.title: Saint Ursula laughs
cues.text: Near 6:45 the music peaks on “Sanct Ursula selbst dazu lacht!” — Saint Ursula herself laughs at it. In the Adagio Mahler pictured her presiding with a smile. A ritardando and a short pause follow, then “a tempo”.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 125: “Sanct Ur-” at the end of the first system, “riten.”, then “-sula selbst da-zu lacht!”, a fermata and “kurz a tempo” at rehearsal 14. Report: relative level is −13.4 dB at 6:40, −10.3 dB at 6:45 and −20.0 dB at 6:50. Mahler’s 1901 description of St Ursula presiding over the Adagio is quoted on the Mahler Foundation’s introduction page: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler at the Welte-Mignon
cues.text: On 9 November 1905 Mahler recorded this finale in a piano version for the Welte-Mignon reproducing piano in Leipzig. The Mahler Foundation lists it first among the symphony’s historical recordings.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s history page lists “09-11-1905 Leipzig. Gustav Mahler. Symphony No. 4 – Movement 4 … Welte-Mignon” as its first historical recording and, separately, a “1905 Recording Leipzig” performance entry: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-history/
cues.how: Documented fact.

cues.title: Cecilia and her musicians
cues.text: In this closing stretch the text names Saint Cecilia, patron of music, and her relatives as “treffliche Hofmusikanten” — splendid court musicians. Harp triplets keep a rocking pulse under muted strings and the voice.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 126 (printed p. 352): “Cä-ci-lia mit ih-ren Ver-wan-ten sind treff-li-che Hof-mu-si-kan-ten!”, harp triplets, muted strings. The page is placed by proportion between the 6:28 boundary and the 7:56 boundary; report: level −15.5 to −13.6 dB at 7:15–7:25.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: So that all awakens to joy
cues.text: The last sung phrase, “dass alles für Freuden erwacht” — so that all may awaken to joy — stretches over long, soft notes. The voice floats above the orchestra, which is now almost still.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 126–127 (printed pp. 352–353): “Die eng-li-schen Stim-men er-mun-tern die Sin-nen”, then “dass Al-les für Freu-den, für Freu-den er-wacht”, pp. Report: boundary at 7:56 (novelty 0.50) and relative level −17 to −20 dB at 7:30–7:55.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sich Zeit lassen
cues.text: With the voice finished, the cor anglais and bass clarinet fade “morendo”, and the harp is told “sich Zeit lassen” — take your time. The low strings sustain under a fermata; the score ends “Ende der Symphonie”.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 127 (printed p. 353), last system: cor anglais and bass clarinet “morendo”, harp “sich Zeit lassen!”, cellos and basses arco ppp, fermata, “Ende der Symphonie.” Report: relative level falls from −22.1 dB at 8:10 to −31.3 dB at 8:25 and −54.7 dB at 8:30 and −79.2 dB at 8:35, near the analysis floor by 8:35–8:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A symphony that ends elsewhere
cues.text: The symphony starts in G major and ends in E major, a progressive tonal scheme. The Mahler Foundation notes that the postlude modulates to E and stays there, ending away from the tonic.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page says that by the postlude there is a modulation to E major, in which the symphony ends away from the G major tonic: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-4-das-himmlische-leben-sehr-behaglich/ . Its introduction describes the progressive scheme: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-introduction/
cues.how: Documented fact.

transitions.title: The voice enters over a hushed band
transitions.how: The prelude ends with a flurry of flutes and clarinets and a “Poco rit.”, then the soprano enters at rehearsal 1, “a tempo”. The orchestra thins at once to clarinets, harp and discreet pizzicato strings, as Mahler’s note to the conductor demands. The voice takes the same gentle tune the clarinets, oboes and flutes had just played, so the song grows out of the prelude rather than interrupting it.
transitions.evidence: Full score (IMSLP70999), PDF pp. 102–104 (printed pp. 328–330): “Poco rit.”, rehearsal 1 “a tempo”, the vocal entry and the note on discreet accompaniment. Basinger says the soprano gives voice to the melody the clarinets, oboes and flutes had played: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: level −11 dB at 0:25 falls to −20.7 dB at 0:30.

transitions.title: Sleigh bells break the chorale
transitions.how: The first verse closes on a hushed, chorale-like “Sanct Peter im Himmel sieht zu”, with muted strings and horns. Then comes “Plötzlich frisch bewegt”: the first movement’s sleigh-bell figure, now in the minor and scored with real sleigh bells, triangle, cymbals and bells-up woodwinds, with the strings striking with the wood of the bow. The shock of colour and tempo is the join; when the voice returns it has a new melody for the lamb and the ox.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 108–109 (printed pp. 334–335): “Plötzlich zurückhaltend”, “Plötzlich frisch bewegt” and the footnote on tempo, “Schalltr. auf”, “mit dem Bogen geschlagen”. Report: level −28.1 dB at 1:45 rising to −10.8 dB at 1:50, boundary at 1:50 (novelty 0.71) and brightness 2891 Hz.

transitions.title: Bells once more, then the first tune
transitions.how: The second verse ends with the angels baking bread and the hymn-like refrain returning. A short instrumental interlude then brings back the distorted sleigh bells, and the soprano resumes with the movement’s first melody for the third verse. Mahler uses the bells as a signpost between verses: the same colour announces each change of scene, while the melody returns to its opening shape.
transitions.evidence: Basinger describes the refrain, the short interlude with distorted sleigh bells and the return of the initial melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: level −27.1 dB at 3:05 and −10.7 dB at 3:10, brightness 2763 Hz at 3:10, G major estimates at 3:20–3:30. The exact bar of the join is not aligned.

transitions.title: The refrain fades; the bells ring
transitions.how: The extended refrain for Saint Martha the cook ebbs away to a very quiet stretch. Then the sleigh bells and triangle sound once more, with fortissimo winds and strings, and fade to pp. At the end of the page the key signature changes to four sharps. The bells mark the last turn of the song, and the descending dynamic prepares the quiet start of the E-major section.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 122 (printed p. 348): “Schellen”, triangle, ff diminishing to pp, and the new signature at the system end. Report: level −21.6 dB at 4:30 and −28.5 dB at 4:45, then −9.4 dB and brightness 2993 Hz at 4:55; boundary at 4:54 (novelty 0.86).

transitions.title: Into E major, tender and mysterious
transitions.how: After the bells, the music settles into E major at rehearsal 12, “Tempo I. Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss”. Flute and cor anglais carry a new, soft version of the movement’s main melody over harp triplets and muted strings with plucked basses. G major, the key of the first three verses, is left behind with no return; the symphony is on its way to ending away from its tonic.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 122–123 (printed pp. 348–349): changed signature, rehearsal 12 “Tempo I. Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schluss”, “mit Dämpfer”, harp triplets, pizzicato basses. Report: boundary at 5:08 (novelty 0.56) and level −24.9 dB at 5:05 and −29.4 dB at 5:10. Basinger on the E major: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

transitions.title: The voice joins the E-major tune
transitions.how: The orchestra has already stated the new melody alone. At rehearsal 13 the soprano takes it up, “Kein’ Musik ist ja nicht auf Erden”, and Mahler repeats the direction “Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schlusse”. The strings stay muted, “immer Dämpfer”, down at ppp, and the harp keeps its triplet rocking, so the voice takes up a prepared melody with the key, the written tempo and the soft, muted character unchanged. The recording’s level does fall slightly around the entry, and the exact bar of the vocal entry is not aligned.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 124 (printed p. 350): rehearsal 13, “Sehr zart und geheimnisvoll bis zum Schlusse”, the vocal line “Kein Mu-sik ist ja nicht auf Erden”, “immer Dämpfer”, ppp, harp triplets. Report: boundary at 6:00 (novelty 0.63), level −23 to −25 dB through 6:10 and attack density near zero.

transitions.title: The last word, then the postlude
transitions.how: The last phrase, “dass alles für Freuden erwacht”, is spread over long, soft notes. With the voice finished, cor anglais and bass clarinet dwindle “morendo”, the harp is told “sich Zeit lassen”, and cellos and basses sustain a quiet note under a fermata. There is no cadence in G and no loud final chord: the movement and the symphony end in E major, by fading rather than by arrival.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 127 (printed p. 353): “dass Al-les für Freu-den, für Freu-den er-wacht”, “morendo”, “sich Zeit lassen!”, fermata and “Ende der Symphonie.” Report: boundaries at 7:56 and 8:08 (novelty 0.50, 0.45); level falls from −22.1 dB at 8:10 to −31.3 dB at 8:25 and −54.7 dB at 8:30 and −79.2 dB at 8:35, near the analysis floor by 8:35–8:40.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, IV. Das himmlische Leben, full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: PDF pp. 102–127 (printed pp. 328–353), rehearsal figures 1–15; changes are placed at the recording’s existing passage anchors and are approximate.

timeline.note: A clarinet and a horn with harp, over muted violas and cellos; violins and basses rest.
Oboes, cor anglais, bass clarinet and bassoons add soft phrases; the basses pluck.
The soprano sings over clarinets, harp and discreet pizzicato strings.
Flutes and clarinets quicken with the voice as the text turns to dancing and singing.
Muted strings and soft horns sustain the chorale-like close to “Sanct Peter”.
Sleigh bells, triangle and bells-up woodwinds rattle in the minor; strings strike with the wood of the bow.
The soprano sings the lamb’s verse to a new melody, with oboe and bass clarinet answering.
The first melody returns for the garden’s herbs and fruit.
The tempo quickens: swirling strings and woodwinds, with brief sleigh bells, for running game and darting fish.
The refrain swells for Saint Martha the cook, then ebbs.
Sleigh bells and triangle ring with fortissimo winds and strings, then fade to pp.
Flute and cor anglais carry the new melody over harp triplets and muted strings; no singer yet.
The soprano takes the new tune over muted strings, harp triplets and soft winds.
Harp triplets rock beneath muted strings and the voice.
Cor anglais and bass clarinet fade; the harp takes its time; cellos and basses sustain softly.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
